title: Counting Clicks
setting: a toad patrol on a country lane

post.author: u/toad_warden_llinos
post.title: I'm the county's night road warden on toad duty. At 01:05 the dashboard closed the lane for the busiest toad hour of the night. It was 2 °C, and toads don't move below 5.

blocks.text: I'm Llinos, the county's night road warden. On warm wet spring nights, toads walk out of the woods, across Withybed Lane, to breed in the reservoir below. A toad patrol meets them: volunteers who carry them over in buckets, each on a stretch of the lane. I wait in the council van. The rule: if volunteers log more than 50 toads crossing in an hour, a closure order comes to my phone, and I put out the barriers.

Volunteers log each toad with one press of a button in the council's app: a tap. First the phone writes down the time by its own clock, the phone clock. Then, with signal, it sends the tap to the council at once. Without signal, it keeps the tap, and sends everything it holds when the volunteer walks back into signal.

A web page of live counts, the council's dashboard, keeps the hourly count. An hour opens on the hour, say 22:00. Each tap that reaches the council is added to the hour that is open. At 23:00 the hour ends, its count is final, and the next opens. Every 5 minutes the dashboard checks the current hour; if it's over 50, it texts me a closure order.

Most toads cross beside the reservoir, and until this year nobody patrolled there. This spring the patrol added that stretch. It dips where no phone has any signal. Teilo and Gurbir took it, 22:00 to 01:00 on the rota, cars parked up the lane where the signal starts. The rota holds the stretch till 01:00 because toads sometimes move again after a lull, and down there nothing could reach them to say otherwise. Their phones would be what Ormerod, who runs the app, calls late phones: holding every tap until they walk back up.

Thursday 5 March was the year's first warm wet night: 8 °C at 21:00, and rain. Toads don't move below about 5 °C. At 22:30 the rain stopped and the cold came down: 5 °C at 23:00, 2 °C at 01:00. The 22:00 hour ended at 12. The lane stayed open.

At 01:05 my phone buzzed with a closure order. I read it under a frosted windscreen: 01:00 hour, 340 crossings, the busiest of the night. The van said 2 °C. I put the barriers across an empty road that glittered.
Three hundred and forty toads, walking through a frost that stops every one of them.
I rang Ormerod at 01:10. At 01:20 he sent me the night's taps. Each line: the phone, the tap time by its phone clock, and the arrival time by the council's clock.

phone   tapped     arrived
14      22:41:07   22:41:08
21      22:03:12   01:00:31
22      22:04:55   01:00:44
...
21      22:58:19   01:00:31
340 taps from phones 21 and 22, tapped 22:00 to 23:00
12 taps from other phones, each arrived within 2 seconds

blocks.label: hobbs_lane_taps_2100_0300.png

diagram.aria: Thursday 5 March 21:00 to Friday 6 March 03:00. The air is above 5 °C until 23:00 and below it after. Toads are tapped only between 22:00 and 23:00. Taps arriving at the council: 12 between 22:00 and 23:00, none from 23:00 to 01:00 while the reservoir phones are out of signal, then 340 between 01:00 and 01:05. Markers: 01:00 the volunteers walk back into signal; 01:05 the closure order.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from Ormerod's export of the night's taps, in 5-minute steps, Thursday 5 March 21:00 to Friday 03:00. Every toad was tapped between 22:00 and 23:00, while the air was over 5 °C. Only 12 taps reached the council that hour (amber). The 340 from phones 21 and 22 waited on the phones until 01:00 (red), and the dashboard counted them in the 01:00 hour.

blocks.text: Nobody did anything wrong. The council meets at 10:00 to decide what the dashboard should change before the next warm night. What should they change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Your log has two times on every line, and both have names. The tap time is the event time: when the thing really happened. The arrival time is the processing time: when the system got it and handled it. Your dashboard sorts taps into hours by one of them. Ask Ormerod two things before 10:00. Did any other taps come in late tonight? And by the rota, what is the longest a phone can be out of signal?

replies.author: u/toad_warden_llinos
replies.text: Ormerod checked. Only the 340 from phones 21 and 22 came in late; every other tap arrived within 2 seconds. No stretch keeps anyone out of signal longer than the reservoir shift: 22:00 to 01:00, 3 hours.

comments.author: u/just_sync_them_bohdan
comments.text: It's right there in the log. Phone 21 says 22:03 and the council got it at 01:00. That's a phone clock three hours out. Cheap phones drift: their clocks run fast or slow until someone corrects them. Sync every phone to the council's clock: the app asks the council for the time and sets the phone to match, before the patrol walks out. Do that and the hours fix themselves.

replies.author: u/toad_warden_llinos
replies.text: Ormerod says the app can sync every phone at the start of each patrol. He could switch it on tonight.

comments.author: u/live_means_live_temitope
comments.text: A tap that turns up three hours after the toad isn't a live count any more, it's history. Counting it at 01:00 is what closed a frozen road. Have the dashboard ignore any tap that arrives more than 10 minutes late. A live count should count live toads.

replies.author: u/toad_warden_llinos
replies.text: Teilo read this over my shoulder and went quiet. Then he said, "So our whole night never happened."

reply.prompt: The council meets at 10:00 on Friday 6 March, and the next warm wet night could be any night now. What should they change on the dashboard? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Count each toad in the hour it was tapped, and hold that hour open for late phones.
options.part2: The council chose it at 10:00, and Ormerod had it running by Tuesday 10 March. Each tap now counts in the hour it was tapped, by the phone clock. Each hour is shown as it goes, stays open for 3 hours after it ends (the longest the rota keeps any phone out of signal), and is final after that. The closure rule watches only the hour it is in. A past hour corrected to over 50 is logged, and the council plans the next warm night from it. In the sim, replaying Thursday 5 March this way: at 23:00 the 22:00 hour is shown as 12 and the lane stays open; at 01:05 Teilo's and Gurbir's 340 taps arrive and correct it to 352; at 02:00 it is final at 352. The 01:00 hour reads 0, and no closure order goes out in the frost. The council logged the 22:00 hour at 352 and planned to close the lane at dusk on the next warm wet night with volunteers at the reservoir. What the change could not do was close the lane at 22:00 on 5 March: at 22:00 the dashboard still knew of only 12.
options.senior: Count each event in the window of when it happened, not when it arrived, and decide on purpose how long to wait for stragglers. Here the wait comes from the rota: no phone is out of signal for more than 3 hours, so each hour stays open 3 hours after it ends, then it is final. Show each hour early and correct it as late taps land, and keep the live decision on the current hour, so a correction to the past updates the record instead of closing a frozen road. Be honest about the limit: counting by tap time gets the record right, but it cannot act on taps it has not received. For a live decision on the reservoir stretch you need the taps sooner (signal, a radio, a runner) or a plan made from past nights.

options.text: Sync every volunteer's phone clock to the council's clock, so the tap times are right.
options.part2: Ormerod switched on clock sync that night: at the start of each patrol, every phone sets its clock from the council's. In the sim, replaying Thursday 5 March with every phone synced: no tap moves, because every phone clock was already within a second of the council's. The 22:00 hour still reads 12, the 340 still arrive at 01:00 and count in the 01:00 hour, and the closure order still goes out at 01:05, at 2 °C. The phones had told the truth all along: Teilo tapped a toad at 22:03, and the tap reached the council at 01:00.
options.senior: Syncing clocks fixes clocks that are wrong. These were right: the gap between 22:03 and 01:00 is not a clock error, it is three hours in a pocket out of signal. Read the evidence before you choose a fix: the tap times all sat inside the warm hour, the arrival times all sat at the moment two people walked into signal. The bug is which of the two times the dashboard counts by. Wrong clocks are a real problem elsewhere ("Never Trust the Clock", s8e05); here every clock in the story was right.

options.text: Ignore any tap that arrives more than 10 minutes late, so old taps cannot pile up.
options.part2: Ormerod set the dashboard to throw away any tap more than 10 minutes late. In the sim, replaying Thursday 5 March: the 340 reservoir taps arrive at 01:00, two to three hours late, and are thrown away. No closure in the frost. The 22:00 hour reads 12, and the night's record says 12 toads crossed. Every warm night after, the reservoir stretch's taps were thrown away the same way, and in April the council, reading a quiet stretch, asked whether it needed patrolling at all.
options.senior: Dropping late data stops it doing harm in the wrong hour by making sure it never counts anywhere. On this lane the late taps are the most important ones: they come from the stretch where most toads cross. A cut-off this short only suits data that is worthless once it is old, such as a live position. A count that records what happened needs late data put in its right place, not thrown away.

options.text: Count every tap once, in the morning, after all the phones have sent theirs in.
options.part2: The council stopped counting live. Each morning at 07:00, with every phone in, the dashboard counts every tap in the hour it was tapped. In the sim, replaying Thursday 5 March: no closure in the frost, and at 07:00 the 22:00 hour reads 352, right first time. Then replay last spring's busiest night, when every stretch had signal: counted live, the 21:00 hour passed 50 and the lane closed at 21:50; counted in the morning, its 64 toads show up at 07:00, and the lane stays open all night while they cross.
options.senior: Waiting until all the data is in gives an exact count, and for a yearly report it is the right tool: a batch job, run once over a finished night. But the rule exists to close a road while toads are on it, and a count that arrives at 07:00 can never do that, even on nights when every phone had signal. Keep the morning count as a check on the record if you like, and keep the live count for the decision.

sim.title: Replay the night on Withybed Lane
sim.lede: You're replaying Thursday 5 March from 21:00 to 03:00 on Friday, in 5-minute steps. As given data: toads crossed only between 22:00 and 23:00. On the reservoir stretch (phones 21 and 22, no signal) the taps per 5 minutes from 22:00 were 14, 22, 30, 36, 40, 42, 38, 34, 30, 24, 18 and 12: 340. They all reached the council between 01:00 and 01:05, when Teilo and Gurbir walked back into signal at the end of their 22:00 to 01:00 shift. On the other stretches, in signal, 12 taps (1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0), each arriving within 2 seconds. Air by the hour: 8, 7, 5, 3, 2, 1 and 0 °C from 21:00 to 03:00; toads don't move below about 5 °C. Every phone clock was within 1 second of the council's. The rule: close the lane when the current hour's count is over 50, checked at the end of every 5-minute step. Count by arrival time (as built) or tap time. With tap time, the watermark is none (each hour is final the moment it ends, and a later tap for it is set aside) or up to 3 hours (each hour stays open 3 hours after it ends, the longest the rota keeps a phone out of signal; a corrected past hour is logged, never a closure). Smoothing checks the average of the current hour and the two before it. The second night is last spring's busiest, every stretch in signal: 64 taps in the 21:00 hour (3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 6, 5, 6, 5, 5, 4) and 30 in the 22:00 hour, air 9, 7, 5, 4, 3, 3 and 2 °C.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play it as built: the 22:00 hour ends at 12, the 01:00 hour reads 340, and the closure order goes out at 01:05 at 2 °C. Switch to tap time with the watermark at up to 3 hours: the 22:00 hour is shown as 12 at 23:00, corrected to 352 at 01:05 and final at 02:00, and nothing closes in the frost. Set the watermark to none and watch the 340 set aside. Try clock sync, then the 10-minute drop, then smoothing (113 at 01:05). Then switch to last spring's busiest night and compare the live count (closed at 21:50) with the morning count.

explain.oneLine: Nothing was wrong with the toads, the phones or the clocks. The dashboard counted each tap in the hour it arrived, not the hour it was tapped. The 340 toads that crossed on the reservoir stretch between 22:00 and 23:00 reached the council at 01:00, when Teilo and Gurbir walked back into signal, and closed the lane in a frost.

steps.title: A tap has two times, and the dashboard counted the wrong one.
steps.text: A tap goes through four steps. A volunteer presses the button as a toad crosses. The phone writes down the time by its own clock: the event time, when it happened. In signal, the phone sends the tap at once; out of signal, it holds it. When the tap reaches the council, the council's clock marks its arrival: the processing time, when the system got it. In signal, the two times are a second apart, so it never mattered which one the dashboard used. Every stretch before this year had signal. The reservoir stretch pulled them three hours apart, and the dashboard counted by arrival: 12 in the 22:00 hour, 340 in the 01:00 hour. It is the same pair of times as the train sensors in "Out of Order" (s4e14), whose updates arrived seconds out of order; here they arrived hours late, and every clock was right.

steps.title: The hour is a window, and a window is a few steps.
steps.text: A stream, data that keeps arriving one piece at a time, never ends, so a count needs edges. A window is a stretch of time the count is cut into; the dashboard's are one hour each, side by side, like pages in a tally book. A window works in four steps. It opens on the hour. Taps fall into it by their time. It closes. Its count is final. Two choices hide in those steps: which time decides the window, and when the window is final. Counted by arrival time, a window is final the moment it ends, because nothing can arrive in the past; the price is that a late tap lands in the wrong hour. Counted by tap time, every tap lands in its own hour, but you have to decide how long to wait for stragglers.

steps.title: Late data, the watermark, and an hour shown early then corrected.
steps.text: Late data is a tap whose hour has already ended when it arrives. A watermark is the system's estimate of how far tap time is complete: "every tap from before 22:05 is in". Nothing can know that for certain, so it is a rule, here taken from the rota: no phone is out of signal for more than 3 hours. So each hour stays open for 3 hours after it ends, and only then is final; that wait is called allowed lateness. Each hour is shown early, as it goes, and corrected as late taps land: the 22:00 hour reads 12 at 23:00, 352 at 01:05, and is final at 352 at 02:00. The 01:00 hour reads 0. The closure rule watches only the current hour, so a correction to the past updates the record and the plan for the next warm night, never the barriers. In the sim with no watermark at all, each hour is final the moment it ends, and the 340 are set aside as too late.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fail, and the walk out to the reservoir.
steps.text: Syncing the phone clocks moves no tap: every clock was within a second, so the 340 still close the lane at 01:05. Throwing away taps over 10 minutes late throws away all 340, and the record says 12 toads crossed. Smoothing over 3 hours averages the 01:00 hour with the two quiet ones before it, 340 over 3 is 113, still over 50, still a frost closure; and on last spring's busiest night, 64 in the 21:00 hour, the average peaks at about 31, so the lane that closed at 21:50 would stay open. A morning count is exact, 352 at 07:00, but it can never close a road while toads are on it. At 07:00 Llinos drove down to where her phone lost its last bar and walked on, down into the dip. The verge by the reservoir was white with frost and the water was full of toads. Here, between 22:00 and 23:00, 340 of them had crossed while the dashboard on the hill counted 12.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for one night. Phones in signal send taps at once; the reservoir phones hold theirs until 01:00. The dashboard puts every tap in the hour it was tapped. The 22:00 hour shows 12 at 23:00, 352 after 01:05, and is final at 02:00. The closure rule looks only at the current hour; a corrected past hour goes to the night record and the plan for the next warm night.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for one night. Every tap goes into the hour it was tapped, however late it arrives. The 22:00 hour is shown as 12 at 23:00, corrected to 352 when the reservoir phones walk back into signal at 01:00, and final at 02:00. The closure rule looks only at the hour it is in, so the correction goes to the night record and the next night's plan, not to the barriers.

fix.title: The fix: count by tap time, hold each hour open 3 hours, and close only on the current hour
fix.text: Put every tap in the hour it was tapped, by the phone clock, not the hour it reached the council. Show each hour as it goes, keep it open for 3 hours after it ends, the longest the rota keeps any phone out of signal, and correct it as late taps arrive; after that the hour is final, and anything later is set aside and reported, not lost. Let the closure rule act only on the current hour. A past hour corrected to over 50 goes into the night record, and the council plans from it: on the next warm wet night with volunteers at the reservoir, the lane closes at dusk. Write the 3 hours down beside the rota, so a longer shift changes both.

limits: Counting by tap time cannot close the lane before the late taps arrive. At 22:00 the dashboard still knew of only 12, and the lane stayed open while 340 toads crossed. Only getting the taps sooner (signal, a radio, a runner) or closing on a plan made from past nights fixes the live decision.

The watermark is a guess. A phone out of signal longer than 3 hours, a flat battery or a longer shift, arrives after its hour is final and is set aside. Keep those taps and report them, so the record can still be corrected.
A count that changes after it is shown needs saying so. People reading 12 at 23:00 must know the hour is still open, or they will act on a number that later becomes 352.

head: How the dashboard counts
Good
Bad
rows: Simple; every hour is final the moment it ends.
22:00 hour 12, 01:00 hour 340; the lane closes at 01:05 at 2 °C.
These were right; nothing moves, still closed at 01:05.
All 340 thrown away; the record says 12 crossed.
Still 113 at 01:05 and a frost closure; last spring's 64 never closes the lane.
No live closure ever, even on nights with signal everywhere.
By tap time, each hour open 3 hours, close on the current hour (the fix)
22:00 hour corrected to 352, 01:00 hour 0, no frost closure.
Cannot close at 22:00 on taps it hasn't got; a phone out over 3 hours is set aside.

explain.seniorTake: Any count over time has to answer two questions: which time decides where an event belongs, and how long you wait before you call a period done. Count by when it happened, because that is what the decision is about. Then pick the wait from what you know about your slowest source, here a 3-hour shift out of signal, and write it down. Show results early and correct them, and keep live actions on fresh windows, so a correction to the past updates the record instead of firing an alarm. Treat the watermark as an estimate that will sometimes be wrong both ways: too short and real data is set aside, too long and the final number comes late. And when a decision has to happen before the data can arrive, no counting method will save it; you need the data sooner or a plan made from the past.

realWorld.title: The Dataflow Model, 2015: data that may never be complete
realWorld.text: Akidau and colleagues at Google open their paper with a warning for anyone counting a stream: "We as a field must stop trying to groom unbounded datasets into finite pools of information that eventually become complete". The dashboard's "final at 23:00" was that assumption.

realWorld.title: Dataflow: two kinds of time
realWorld.text: The paper names the two times on every tap. Event time is "the time at which the event itself actually occurred"; processing time is "the time at which an event is observed at any given point during processing within the pipeline". The dashboard counted the second.

realWorld.title: Dataflow: a phone in the wilderness
realWorld.text: The paper's own example is a phone out of signal: "If someone takes their mobile device into the wilderness, the system has no practical way of knowing when they might come back to civilization, regain connection, and begin uploading data about video views during that time." So "most watermarks must be heuristically defined based on limited knowledge available". Withybed Lane's 3 hours is such an estimate, taken from the rota.

realWorld.title: Dataflow: watermarks too fast and too slow
realWorld.text: The authors list two failings of a watermark. "They are sometimes too fast, meaning there may be late data that arrives behind the watermark." And too slow: "the watermark can be held back for the entire pipeline by a single slow datum." Too short a wait sets toads aside; too long a wait makes every night's final count late.

realWorld.title: Dataflow: results that refine themselves
realWorld.text: Among the ways the model lets a window report more than once, it describes accumulating results, where "later results become a refinement of previous results". The 22:00 hour shown as 12 at 23:00 and as 352 at 01:05 is exactly that.

realWorld.title: Apache Flink: event time and processing time
realWorld.text: Flink's "Timely Stream Processing" page: "Event time is the time that each individual event occurred on its producing device." And: "Processing time refers to the system time of the machine that is executing the respective operation." A volunteer's phone is the producing device.

realWorld.title: Apache Flink: watermarks and late elements
realWorld.text: The same page: "A Watermark(t) declares that event time has reached time t in that stream". And: "Late elements are elements that arrive after the system’s event time clock" has passed their time. It notes that counts on streams are cut into windows: "Windows can be time driven (example: every 30 seconds) or data driven (example: every 100 elements)." The dashboard's hours are time driven.

asked: Event time or processing time: which would you count by?
How do you handle late data in a streaming count?
interview.answer: Event time is when something happened, recorded by the device; processing time is when my system received or handled it. For anything that describes the world, counts per hour, sums per day, I count by event time, because processing time mixes in every delay in the network and every device that was offline. That raises the real question: when is a window done? A watermark is the system's estimate that all events up to some time have arrived, and it is always a guess, usually built from what I know about the slowest source. I'd set an allowed lateness from that knowledge, show each window's result early, and update it as late events arrive until the window is final. Anything later still goes to a side list that is reported and can correct the record, not silently dropped. I'd keep live actions, alerts and closures, on the current window, so a correction to the past updates reports instead of firing an alarm. And I'd be honest that event time does not make late data early: if a decision needs data before it can arrive, the fix is getting the data sooner or deciding from history. I'd tell the story of a toad-crossing dashboard that counted by arrival, so 340 toads tapped out of signal at 22:00 closed a road at 01:05 in a frost.

Data that keeps arriving one piece at a time and never ends, like taps on a patrol night, handled as it comes instead of all at once.
A stretch of time a stream's count is cut into, like a page in a tally book. The dashboard's windows are one hour each, side by side.

A piece of data that arrives after its window has ended, such as a tap made at 22:03 that reached the council at 01:00.
The system's estimate of how far event time is complete: every tap from before this moment is in. It is a guess, here taken from the 3-hour rota.
How long a window stays open after it ends, to take late data: 3 hours on Withybed Lane, so the 22:00 hour is final at 02:00.

Checking the average of the last few hours instead of the current one. Over 3 hours: 340 over 3 is 113 at 01:05, still over 50.

A job that gathers a finished stretch of data, such as one whole night of taps, and handles it in one go, like the morning count.

Free software for processing streams, one event at a time, with care for when each event really happened (s9e07).

The SOC 2 area about processing being complete, valid, accurate and on time. For the dashboard: each toad counted once, in the hour it crossed.

atWork: Find every dashboard, alert or report that counts events per minute, hour or day, and ask which time it counts by: when the event happened, or when it reached you. Then find the devices that can go quiet and send later: phones in poor signal, card readers on a train, sensors on a ship, apps used offline. A dashboard that counts by arrival while some devices send late is a common pattern, and it hides until the first busy night those devices are offline; then a quiet hour looks quieter and a later hour looks impossible. For each count, write down which time it uses, how late your slowest source can be, how long each window stays open before it is final, and what happens to anything later still. Keep alerts and live decisions on the current window, and let late data correct the record, not fire the alarm. Standards, stated conditionally: if your company is pursuing SOC 2 with the processing integrity criteria (PI1), an auditor would usually look for evidence that processing is complete, valid, accurate and timely, here that each event is counted once and in the period it happened, with late or set-aside data reported rather than silently dropped. Build the choice of time and the late-data rule into the first design rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your company makes running watches. Each watch saves a run and sends it to your servers the next time it reaches its owner's phone. A live dashboard shows runs started per hour in each town. On Sunday a hill race starts at 09:00; 1,400 runners carry their phones, but there is no signal on the hill, and they get it back in town at 15:00. The dashboard shows 3 runs started in the 09:00 hour and 1,400 in the 15:00 hour, and the race office asks why everyone set off at three in the afternoon. What happened, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The dashboard counts runs in the hour they reached the servers (processing time), not the hour they started (event time)
Count each run by when it started (event time), keeping each hour open for late arrivals
Show each hour early and correct it as late runs land, with a stated limit after which the hour is final

recall.model: The watches were right about when each run started; the dashboard counted by processing time, the hour each run reached the servers, and the runners only got signal back in town at 15:00. So the 09:00 hour looked empty and the 15:00 hour impossible. I'd count each run by event time, the start time the watch recorded, and keep each hour open for late arrivals: a watermark based on how long a watch can realistically be out of reach, perhaps a day. Each hour is shown early and updated as late runs come in, and is final only once that wait has passed; anything later still is set aside and reported, not silently dropped. Any alert should act only on the current hour, so a correction to the past updates the record without firing.

recall.prompt: With the fix (count by tap time, each hour open 3 hours after it ends), what does the 22:00 hour show on 5 March, and when?
options: 12 at 23:00, final at 12, because the hour ended at 23:00
12 at 23:00, then 352 at 01:05, final at 352 at 02:00
352 at 23:00, because every toad crossed in that hour
0 at 23:00, then 340 at 01:05, final at 340 at 02:00
recall.why: Only 12 taps had arrived by 23:00, so the hour is first shown as 12. The 340 reservoir taps arrive at 01:00, inside the 3 hours the hour stays open, and correct it to 352 at the 01:05 check. At 02:00, 3 hours after it ended, it is final. Final at 12 is the hour with no watermark; 352 at 23:00 would need taps that hadn't arrived.

recall.prompt: Which of these is a watermark in stream processing?
options: A stamp on each event showing which device sent it
A limit that throws away any event more than 10 minutes old
The system's estimate that all events up to some time have arrived, so a window up to then can be called complete
A copy of every event kept for a later check
recall.why: A watermark is an estimate of how far event time is complete: everything from before this point is in. Windows ending before it can be treated as final. It is a guess, usually built from what you know about the slowest source; a fixed drop rule throws data away instead, and a device stamp says who, not when.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: what is the difference between event time and processing time, and how should a streaming count handle late data?

keyIdeas.idea: Event time is when it happened on the device; processing time is when the system received or handled it
Count in windows by when it happened, wait a stated time for stragglers (a watermark and allowed lateness), and update results as late events land
The wait is a trade-off: too short sets real data aside, too long makes results late; anything later still is reported, not silently lost

recall.model: Event time is when something happened, recorded on the device; processing time is when the system received or handled it, which adds every delay along the way. For counts that describe the world, I count by when it happened, in windows such as one hour. Since events can arrive late, I need a rule for when a window is done: a watermark, the system's estimate that everything up to some time is in, plus allowed lateness, how long a window stays open after it ends. I show each window early and update it as late events land until it is final. Choosing the wait is a trade-off: too short and real data is set aside, too long and final results come late, as the Dataflow paper puts it, watermarks can be too fast or too slow. Anything later still goes to a side list that is reported, not silently dropped, and alerts act only on the current window.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 1 month later. Since Tuesday 10 March the dashboard counts each tap in the hour it was tapped and keeps each hour open for 3 hours after it ends. No more frost closures. On Wednesday 1 April, a warm wet night, Eldrid joined Teilo on the reservoir stretch, 22:00 to 01:00. Her phone's battery died at 22:40, and she charged it at home. At 08:15 on Thursday 2 April it sent her 80 taps, all made between 22:00 and 22:40. The dashboard set all 80 aside as too late, and the night record says the 22:00 hour had 61 toads.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why are Eldrid's 80 toads missing from the night record, and what should the council change?

keyIdeas.idea: Her taps arrived after the 22:00 hour was final at 02:00: the 3-hour wait is an estimate, and a dead battery beat it
Don't lose set-aside taps: keep them and correct the record afterwards (a morning re-count over every tap)
Let the phones help the estimate: a phone that hasn't reported in since its shift keeps the hour open, or is followed up

coldCase.model: Eldrid's taps came in at 08:15, long after the 22:00 hour was final at 02:00, so the dashboard set them aside: the 3-hour wait is an estimate, built from the rota, and a dead battery beat it. The live count was never going to see them in time, and that's fine; the record is what is wrong. Two changes. First, keep set-aside taps and correct the record afterwards: a morning re-count over every tap, by tap time, would put the 22:00 hour at 141, and the corrected figure is what the council should plan from. Second, let the phones improve the estimate: every phone on the rota checks in when it is back in signal, so the dashboard knows which phones still hold taps; one that hasn't reported in by the end of its shift is followed up, or keeps its hour open a little longer.
